targets.title: Challenges in the Decentralised Web: The Mastodon Case
targets.authors: Aravindh Raman, Sagar Joglekar, Emiliano De Cristofaro, Nishanth Sastry, Gareth Tyson
targets.why_needed: Crawls the Mastodon fediverse and measures how instance-level federation concentrates users and posts on a small number of servers and autonomous systems, then simulates outages at the largest ones. Supplies the measured cost of instance-level defederation as a moderation and durability mechanism, which the domain brief asks to compare against composable labelers.

targets.title: Bluesky and the AT Protocol: Usable Decentralized Social Media
targets.authors: Martin Kleppmann, Paul Frazee, Jake Gold, Jay Graber, Daniel Holmgren, Devin Ivy, Jeromy Johnson, Bryan Newbold, Jaz Volpert
targets.venue: ACM CoNEXT Workshop on the Decentralization of the Internet (DIN)
targets.why_needed: The system paper by the AT Protocol's own designers, describing feed generators (independent services that any party runs, that produce a ranked list of post URIs a client requests and renders) and the separation of hosting, indexing (relays), and labeling as distinct swappable roles. This is the primary description of the client-selected-ranking mechanism the domain brief needs specified precisely enough to implement.

targets.title: Looking AT the Blue Skies of Bluesky
targets.authors: Leonhard Balduf, Saidu Sokoto, Onur Ascigil, Gareth Tyson, Björn Scheuermann, Maciej Korczyński, Ignacio Castro, Michał Król
targets.why_needed: Independent crawl-based measurement of the deployed AT Protocol network, cataloguing the population of feed generators, the relay operators that index the whole firehose, and the labeling services in production, with counts of who actually operates each role. Needed to check whether feed generation is concretely decentralized in practice or concentrated among a few operators, since a role being technically swappable does not mean it is actually diverse.

targets.title: Bluesky: Network topology, polarization, and algorithmic curation
targets.authors: Dorian Quelle, Alexandre Bovet
targets.why_needed: Reports that of roughly 5 million measured Bluesky accounts, about 139,000 (approximately 2.8%) had liked at least one non-default feed, i.e. had ever engaged with an alternative to the platform-supplied default. This is the direct measured answer the domain brief asks for on what fraction of users actually change a default ranking setting, which decides whether client-selected ranking changes real user exposure or stays a capability nobody exercises.

targets.title: Whose Posts Get Ranked: Identical-Text Exposure Gaps in Bluesky Custom Feeds
targets.authors: Yipeng Wang, Mohit Singhal
targets.why_needed: Repeatedly snapshots the Top-50 lists of 1,366 public Bluesky custom feeds and finds that for identical post text, one copy appears on a feed's ranked list while another copy does not in roughly a third of cases, correlated with the posting account's prior history on that specific feed. This is a measured failure condition of client-selected, third-party ranking: two mechanically identical inputs receive different exposure, which any ranking-without-a-global-index selection must account for.

targets.title: Understanding Decentralized Social Feed Curation on Mastodon
targets.authors: Yuhan Liu, Emmy Song, Owen Xingjian Zhang, Jewel Merriman, Lei Zhang, Andrés Monroy-Hernández
targets.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW)
targets.why_needed: Studies how Mastodon users construct and share feed-curation practices (lists, hashtag following, third-party tools) in the absence of any platform-supplied ranking algorithm, i.e. the reverse-chronological-only baseline against which Bluesky's feed-generator marketplace is a contrast. Needed to establish what unranked, no-global-index feed consumption looks like in a deployed system of comparable scale.

targets.title: Flocking to Mastodon: Tracking the Great Twitter Migration
targets.authors: Jiahui He, Haris Bin Zia, Ignacio Castro, Aravindh Raman, Nishanth Sastry, Gareth Tyson
targets.why_needed: Measures the 2022 Twitter-to-Mastodon migration cohort at scale: which instances absorbed the new accounts, how quickly newcomers left again, and how instance choice concentrated. Supplies measured churn and concentration numbers for a real onboarding event onto a federated system, which any decentralized-web client claiming to reproduce mainstream-platform usage patterns needs as a baseline for what happens when a large cohort arrives at once.

targets.title: An Exploration of Decentralized Moderation on Mastodon
targets.authors: Carlo Alberto Bono, Lucio La Cava, Luca Luceri, Francesco Pierri
targets.why_needed: Measures moderation actions (suspensions, silences, defederations) actually issued by Mastodon instance administrators and characterizes which instances issue them, at what rate, and against which targets. Supplies the measured baseline for instance-level, admin-issued moderation that a composable-labeler design is proposed as a replacement for.

targets.title: Will Admins Cope? Decentralized Moderation in the Fediverse
targets.authors: Ishaku Hassan Anaobi, Aravindh Raman, Ignacio Castro, Haris Bin Zia, Damilola Ibosiola, Gareth Tyson
targets.venue: Proceedings of the ACM Web Conference (WWW)
targets.why_needed: Measures the moderation workload carried by individual Mastodon instance administrators as the fediverse grew after the 2022 Twitter migration, quantifying reports handled per admin and the tooling gaps admins report. This is the measured cost side of instance-operator-driven moderation, needed to compare against the operating cost of composable labeler services run by dedicated parties.

targets.title: Self-moderation in the Decentralized Era: Decoding Blocking Behavior on Bluesky
targets.authors: Carlo Bono, Nick Liu, Giuseppe Russo, Francesco Pierri
targets.venue: Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM)
targets.why_needed: Measures individual-account blocking on Bluesky at scale: who blocks whom, how block relationships cluster, and how blocking functions as a per-user moderation signal distinct from both instance-level defederation and labeler subscription. Needed as the measured behavior of the third moderation primitive (individual user block lists) alongside instance blocking and composable labelers.

targets.title: "A Blocklist is a Boundary": Tensions between Community Protection and Mutual Aid on Federated Social Networks
targets.authors: Erika Melder, Ada Lerner, Michael Ann DeVito
targets.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CHI)
targets.why_needed: Interview-based study of fediverse blocklist curators, server operators, and affected users that identifies the specific failure condition of shared community-level blocklists: federation encodes default-on interaction and instance-level block decisions cut off users who had no part in making them, severing mutual-aid ties. Supplies the measured (interview-derived) failure mode of shared block lists as a fact distinct from any judgment about whether to use them.

targets.title: Understanding Community-Level Blocklists in Decentralized Social Media
targets.authors: Owen Xingjian Zhang, Sohyeon Hwang, Yuhan Liu, Manoel Horta Ribeiro, Andrés Monroy-Hernández
targets.why_needed: Measures how shared instance blocklists propagate and get adopted across Mastodon instances, and quantifies how much of the network a given blocklist's adoption actually isolates. Supplies the measured reach and adoption pattern of the shared-blocklist mechanism, complementing the qualitative failure modes in Melder et al.

targets.title: Collaborative Content Moderation in the Fediverse
targets.authors: Haris Bin Zia, Aravindh Raman, Ignacio Castro, Gareth Tyson
targets.why_needed: Proposes and evaluates a moderation architecture in which instances share moderation signals (not final decisions) with each other rather than each instance moderating in isolation or defederating wholesale. A competing point in the moderation-architecture design space against both Bluesky-style composable labelers and Mastodon-style unilateral instance blocking, with its own measured tradeoffs.

targets.title: On the Effects of Decentralized Moderation on Network Robustness and Information Diffusion in Mastodon
targets.authors: Beatriz Arregui-García, Lucio La Cava, Anees Baqir, Andrea Tagarelli, Riccardo Gallotti, Sandro Meloni
targets.why_needed: Measures how instance-level defederation changes the connectivity and information-flow properties of the fediverse graph, i.e. the structural consequence of decentralized moderation decisions on the network as a whole rather than only on the instance that issues them. Needed to check whether moderation decisions made locally by one instance operator degrade reachability for accounts on unrelated instances.

targets.title: Trouble in Paradise? Understanding Mastodon Admin's Motivations, Experiences, and Challenges Running Decentralised Social Media
targets.authors: Zhilin Zhang, Jun Zhao, Ge Wang, Samantha-Kaye Johnston, George Chalhoub, Tala Ross, Diyi Liu, Claudine Tinsman, Rui Zhao, Max Van Kleek, Nigel Shadbolt
targets.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW)
targets.why_needed: Interviews 16 Mastodon instance administrators on why they run an instance, what moderation and infrastructure work that requires, and where they say the software gives them no adequate tooling. Supplies the measured (interview-derived) operating cost of being a moderation-and-hosting operator under the instance model, which any design replacing instance operators with a different moderation locus must match or beat.

targets.title: Understanding and Improving Content Moderation in Web3 Platforms
targets.authors: Wenrui Zuo, Raul J. Mondragón, Aravindh Raman, Gareth Tyson
targets.venue: Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM)
targets.why_needed: Measures user-driven moderation on the blockchain-based microblogging platform memo.cash from 391,000 posts, and finds platform action count (not content features like hate speech) is the strongest predictor of a post being hidden, with the follower graph controlling visibility. This is a measured moderation-signal population from a platform with no instance operators at all, a data point the fediverse-only moderation literature does not cover.

targets.title: Decentralised Moderation for Interoperable Social Networks: A Conversation-Based Approach for Pleroma and the Fediverse
targets.authors: Vibhor Agarwal, Aravindh Raman, Nishanth Sastry, Ahmed M. Abdelmoniem, Gareth Tyson, Ignacio Castro
targets.venue: Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM)
targets.why_needed: Proposes moderating at the level of a conversation thread rather than a whole instance or a whole account, evaluated on Pleroma fediverse data, as a finer-grained alternative to both instance defederation and account-level blocking. A third competing point in the moderation-granularity design space, with its own measured precision/recall against the other two.

targets.title: An Empirical Analysis of the Nostr Social Network: Decentralization, Availability, and Replication Overhead
targets.authors: Yiluo Wei, Gareth Tyson
targets.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Networking
targets.why_needed: Measures the Nostr protocol's relay-based architecture, in which any relay can hold and serve any user's posts with no assigned home server, quantifying relay availability, financial sustainability, and the message-replication overhead this no-fixed-index design produces. Supplies measured cost figures for a feed-distribution model that is even less centrally indexed than Bluesky's relay/feed-generator split or Mastodon's instance model.

targets.title: Decentralized Recommendation Based on Matrix Factorization: A Comparison of Gossip and Federated Learning
targets.authors: István Hegedűs, Gábor Danner, Márk Jelasity
targets.venue: ECML PKDD Workshops (Machine Learning and Knowledge Discovery in Databases)
targets.why_needed: Implements matrix-factorization collaborative filtering under two decentralized training regimes — gossip learning, in which a model random-walks between peers and each peer updates it with its own local ratings, versus federated learning, in which a coordinating server aggregates peer-computed updates — on the same recommendation task, and measures convergence speed and accuracy of each against each other and against a centralized baseline. Directly supplies the comparison the domain needs between the two leading decentralized-recommendation training architectures.

targets.title: A peer-to-peer recommender system for self-emerging user communities based on gossip overlays
targets.authors: Ranieri Baraglia, Patrizio Dazzi, Matteo Mordacchini, Laura Ricci
targets.venue: Journal of Computer and System Sciences
targets.why_needed: Defines a recommender architecture (PREGO/T-Man derived) in which each peer maintains a gossip overlay linking it to peers with similar interest profiles, discovered purely from repeated pairwise gossip exchange with no server-side index or global item catalogue, and item recommendations are then drawn from a peer's overlay neighborhood. This is a foundational, fully peer-to-peer (not client/server-federated) construction for the class of mechanisms the domain must cover, distinct from and earlier than the gossip-vs-federated comparison in Hegedűs et al.

targets.title: G-Rank: Unsupervised Continuous Learn-to-Rank for Edge Devices in a P2P Network
targets.authors: Andrew Gold, Johan Pouwelse
targets.why_needed: Defines a ranking method that runs entirely on each requesting peer's own device, using only signals available locally (the peer's own click and dwell behavior) plus content received from other peers, with no shared training data, no central model, and no query sent to any index-holding party. This is the direct foundational mechanism for 'ranking without a global index' the domain brief names as underexplored, from the same research group (TU Delft/Tribler) responsible for the already-verified 4P search system.

targets.title: CoolStreaming/DONet: A Data-Driven Overlay Network for Peer-to-Peer Live Media Streaming
targets.authors: Xinyan Zhang, Jiangchuan Liu, Bo Li, Tak-Shing Peter Yum
targets.why_needed: Defines DONet, a mesh-based (not tree-based) live-streaming overlay in which every peer periodically exchanges a data-availability map with a randomly chosen subset of partners and pulls missing pieces from whichever partner holds them, with no fixed relay-tree structure to rebuild on partner departure. The foundational data-driven alternative to relay-tree multicast (Narada, SplitStream) that the domain's peer-assisted-video and live-relay coverage must include, since CoolStreaming was an actually deployed system with a large historical user base.

targets.title: A Measurement Study of a Large-Scale P2P IPTV System
targets.authors: Xiaojun Hei, Chao Liang, Jian Liang, Yong Liu, Keith W. Ross
targets.why_needed: Measures the deployed PPLive P2P IPTV system by crawling and packet-capturing live sessions: peer population per channel, the fraction of a peer's received video segments that actually come from other peers versus from dedicated servers, and how streaming continuity depends on the number of active neighbor peers. Supplies the measured peer-carried-load fraction the domain brief specifically asks for, from an actually deployed system rather than a testbed.

targets.title: SplitStream: High-Bandwidth Multicast in Cooperative Environments
targets.authors: Miguel Castro, Peter Druschel, Anne-Marie Kermarrec, Animesh Nandi, Antony Rowstron, Atul Singh
targets.venue: ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP)
targets.why_needed: Defines a live-streaming relay-tree construction in which the stream is striped into k stripes, each distributed over its own multicast tree built on a Pastry DHT, with trees constructed so that no single peer is an interior (forwarding) node in more than one tree. This bounds any one peer's forwarding load to at most one stripe's worth of bandwidth and survives a peer's departure by only breaking the trees where that peer was interior. The foundational interior-node-disjoint relay-tree mechanism the domain's live-streaming-relay-tree coverage must include, as the structured counterpart to CoolStreaming's unstructured mesh.

targets.title: A Case for End System Multicast
targets.authors: Yang-hua Chu, Sanjay G. Rao, Srinivasan Seshan, Hui Zhang
targets.venue: IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications
targets.why_needed: Defines Narada, in which participating end hosts (not routers) self-organize into a mesh overlay by exchanging membership and performance information, then run a distributed shortest-path computation over that mesh to derive per-source relay trees, with each host reoptimizing its mesh links as measured latency and loss to its current neighbors change. The foundational end-host-only (no router or dedicated-server support required) relay-tree construction, and the direct ancestor of the mesh-first, tree-second design pattern CoolStreaming and SplitStream both build on.

targets.title: ISP-friendly Peer-assisted On-demand Streaming of Long Duration Content in BBC iPlayer
targets.authors: Dmytro Karamshuk, Nishanth Sastry, Andrew Secker, Jigna Chandaria
targets.why_needed: Measures a real BBC iPlayer deployment in which viewers of long-duration video-on-demand content forward already-downloaded segments to other nearby viewers, reporting the achieved fraction of total delivered bytes that peers carried versus what the origin/CDN served, broken out by content duration and by how the peer-assist scheduler was constrained to stay ISP-friendly (favoring same-ISP peers to avoid transit costs). One of the few measured peer-carried-load fractions from a production peer-assisted VoD deployment rather than a testbed or simulation.

targets.title: Stealthy Peers: Understanding Security Risks of WebRTC-Based Peer-Assisted Video Streaming
targets.authors: Siyuan Tang, Eihal Alowaisheq, Xianghang Mi, Yi Chen, XiaoFeng Wang, Yanzhi Dou
targets.why_needed: Analyzes deployed WebRTC-based peer-assisted video-streaming services and demonstrates that a peer participating in delivery can be made to reveal the IP addresses and viewing activity of the other peers it is exchanging segments with, an exposure the WebRTC signaling and ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment) candidate-exchange process was not designed to prevent. The measured attack and its exposed information are the specific fact any WebRTC-assisted-HLS selection for this domain must account for, independent of any vendor's own risk judgment.

targets.title: WebRTC-based peer assisted framework for HTTP live streaming
targets.authors: Midhul Varma, Hema Kumar Yarnagula, Venkatesh Tamarapalli
targets.venue: International Conference on Communication Systems and Networks (COMSNETS)
targets.why_needed: Implements HTTP Live Streaming segment delivery in which a browser fetches a segment from a nearby peer over a WebRTC data channel before falling back to the origin server, and reports the measured fraction of segment requests served by peers versus origin. Directly supplies the domain-requested measured result for 'WebRTC-assisted HLS,' the specific mechanism combination the brief names.

targets.title: Measuring Decentralized Video Streaming: A Case Study of DTube
targets.authors: Trinh Viet Doan, Tat Dat Pham, Markus Oberprieler, Vaibhav Bajpai
targets.why_needed: Measures DTube, a video-sharing platform that stores video content on IPFS (content-addressed storage) and records metadata on a blockchain rather than serving from any operator-controlled server, quantifying retrieval latency, content availability over time, and how much retrieval actually flows peer-to-peer versus through IPFS gateway servers acting as a centralizing chokepoint. Supplies a measured, non-fediverse peer-assisted video deployment as a comparison point against PeerTube.

targets.title: The Centralization of a Decentralized Video Platform: A First Characterization Of PeerTube
targets.authors: Michael Polinski, Richard Jo, Kevin McAfee, Fabián E. Bustamante
targets.why_needed: Crawls the deployed PeerTube network (federated ActivityPub video instances, each independently choosing whether to run WebRTC/HLS peer-assisted delivery) and measures that instance hosting concentrates geographically (roughly 70% of instances in Germany, the USA, and France) and that over 92% of videos are stored on exactly one instance with none of PeerTube's supported redundancy in use. Supplies the measured redundancy-adoption rate and geographic-concentration figures for a deployed federated video platform, distinct from any judgment about whether federation achieved its decentralization goal.

notes: SwarmSearch (arXiv 2505.07452, 'Decentralized Search Engine with Self-Funding Economy') exists as a real preprint and resolves the open question in BRIEF.md section 8 about whether it exists; it belongs to domain B (distributed indexing/search), not K, so it is not listed as a K target here but should be handed to whoever owns B. Livepeer has no peer-reviewed academic measurement paper findable through DBLP, Crossref, or web search as of this pass; everything available is project documentation and blog posts, which the evidence-file rule in BRIEF.md section 2.1 excludes from measured-fact status, so it is omitted from this target list rather than included on documentation alone. No formal academic measurement paper of PeerTube's own WebRTC/HLS peer-assist mechanism in isolation was found (Polinski et al. measures redundancy and centralization, not the peer-assist delivery path itself); a later pass should check PeerTube's own project blog/GitHub for any self-reported peer-assist offload numbers and flag them as project-reported, not independently measured, if used at all. The Bluesky/AT Protocol literature is unusually dense for 2024-2026 and several adjacent papers were found but excluded here as lower-priority than the 22 Bluesky-adjacent and video/moderation targets kept: 'MurkySky: Analyzing News Reliability on Bluesky' (arXiv 2501.10557) and 'A longitudinal analysis of misinformation, polarization and toxicity on Bluesky after its public launch' (arXiv 2505.02317) both bear on ranking/moderation outcomes and are worth a forward-mining pass if evidence extraction finds a gap. VARMA-COMSNETS-17 is a short (2-page) IEEE conference paper; its candidate URLs are both paywalled (IEEE Xplore, ResearchGate request-only) and a later pass should escalate to the authors' IIT Guwahati institutional page or a technical-report version before treating it as unretrievable. ZHANG-ARXIV-25 (community-level blocklists) and ARREGUI-GARCIA-ARXIV-26 (decentralized moderation network effects) have no DOI or venue beyond the arXiv preprint as of this pass; re-check DBLP for a venue assignment before the evidence-extraction pass, since a published version may carry additional peer-reviewed results not in the preprint. All 29 candidate URLs actually resolved (curl HTTP 200) were spot-checked, not all 29; specifically confirmed live during this pass: the PeerTube PDF at privacy-backplane.org, the CoolStreaming PDF at cs.sfu.ca, the Hegedus/Danner/Jelasity PDF at inf.u-szeged.hu, the DTube PDF at dl.ifip.org, the End System Multicast mirror at cs.ucf.edu, and the PPLive measurement PDF at NYU. The remaining URLs are DOI links or arXiv abstract pages, which are reliable by construction rather than needing a spot check. dblp.org intermittently returned connection resets and one 503 during this session (transient, not a persistent block); where a dblp lookup failed I verified via Crossref or the paper's own arXiv listing instead and recorded which route was used in citation_verified_via. The domain brief's example question about what fraction of users change a default ranking setting is answered directly by QUELLE-PLOSONE-25's 2.8% figure (139,000 of ~5,000,000 measured accounts had liked at least one non-default Bluesky feed) — this is the single most load-bearing number found in this pass for the 'is client-selected ranking real' question, and it should not be restated from this note in a later document without opening the primary source, per BRIEF.md section 2.1's own rule.
